Consult Summary:
- 40-year-old woman with ~3 weeks of progressive left-sided hearing reduction and persistent left-sided facial numbness (around the ear and jawline); clinician recommended urgent face-to-face neurological and ear assessment. Differential includes vestibular schwannoma, inner ear inflammatory processes, and viral cranial neuropathy.

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - ~3 weeks of left-sided reduced hearing and persistent numbness on left side of face (around left ear and jawline).
  - Occasional tinnitus (ringing) and intermittent dizziness associated with ringing.
  - Symptoms impacting work (jockey) due to dizziness; gradually affecting training.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No ear pain, no ear discharge, no fever.
  - No generalized body weakness, no difficulty swallowing, no speech difficulty, no vision problems.
  - Numbness is ongoing and present at time of video consult.
- Pertinent negatives (as stated by patient):
  - No ear pain or discharge; no fever; no facial weakness reported; no other neurological deficits described.
- Past medical history, allergies, medications:
  - Past: nasal polyps (intermittent symptoms); remote history patient recalls as “labyrinthitis.”
  - Medications: intermittent prescription nasal steroid spray (name unknown), occasional antacid (Rennies).
  - Allergies: latex.
- Social / preventive health:
  - Occupation: jockey; lives with partner.
  - Family history: brother with neurofibromatosis (type unspecified).
  - Smoking / alcohol not documented.

Examination:
- Vitals: none recorded.
- Physical / observed findings from video consult:
  - Patient reports persistent left facial numbness at time of visit.
  - No observed or reported facial weakness on video.
  - No ear discharge or visible ear complaints reported.
  - No formal neurological or otologic examination performed due to video visit.
- Planned in-person assessments: clinician requested same-day face-to-face clinic for neurological examination and otoscopic inspection of the ear.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression:
  - Acute/subacute unilateral auditory and ipsilateral facial sensory disturbance; etiology currently uncertain.
  - Clinician (on call) suggested Bell’s palsy as a possible diagnosis pending physical exam.
- Differential diagnoses (top 2–3 from DDx, aligned with transcript):
  1. Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) — Medium–High likelihood:
     - Rationale: unilateral progressive hearing loss and tinnitus over weeks with ipsilateral facial sensory disturbance; family history of neurofibromatosis increases suspicion for schwannoma (DDx).
     - Note: no audiometry or imaging yet to confirm.
  2. Labyrinthitis / vestibular neuritis — Medium likelihood:
     - Rationale: prior history of labyrinthitis and current unilateral hearing change with tinnitus and intermittent dizziness; peripheral inner-ear process is plausible.
     - Opposing feature: facial numbness is atypical for isolated labyrinthitis.
  3. Ramsay Hunt syndrome / viral cranial neuropathy or Bell’s-palsy–type process — Low–Medium likelihood:
     - Rationale: clinician raised Bell’s palsy as a possibility; Ramsay Hunt can cause ear/hearing/vestibular symptoms and facial nerve involvement.
     - Opposing features: no documented ear pain, vesicular rash, or facial motor weakness on history.
- Conflict noted:
  - Transcript: clinician suggested Bell’s palsy as a possible diagnosis.
  - DDx ranking: vestibular schwannoma is the highest-ranked diagnosis. Conflict noted between clinician’s preliminary suggestion (Bell’s palsy) and the DDx prioritization.

Plan:
- Immediate actions from transcript:
  - Arrange same-day face-to-face assessment in clinic (neurological examination and ear inspection/otoscopy). Patient instructed to contact support team number and clinic admin to be slotted into an appointment today.
- Recommended next steps consistent with DDx and clinical context (to be performed if in-person exam indicates):
  - Formal neurological cranial-nerve examination and otoscopic exam (to be completed at in-person visit).
  - Formal audiometry (pure-tone and speech audiometry) to characterize hearing loss (sensorineural vs conductive).
  - Consider MRI brain with attention to the cerebellopontine angle (contrast MRI) if exam/audiometry suggest a retrocochlear/compressive lesion (e.g., vestibular schwannoma).
  - ENT and/or neurology referral as indicated by in-person findings.
- Safety advice / follow-up:
  - Urgent same-day in-person assessment emphasized by clinician.
  - Return/seek urgent care if new or worsening symptoms develop: new facial weakness, marked worsening hearing, severe or progressive dizziness/imbalance, vision changes, difficulty swallowing, fever, or other focal neurological signs.
- No medications or procedures were prescribed during the video consult.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs and objective in-person neurological and otologic exam findings.
  - Formal audiometry/her hearing thresholds.
  - Imaging results (MRI) if performed.
  - Exact name/dose/route of nasal spray and complete medication list.
  - Smoking, alcohol, and other relevant social history.
  - Type of family neurofibromatosis (NF1 vs NF2) and documentation of familial testing.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Transcript: clinician suggested Bell’s palsy as a possible diagnosis.
  - DDx: ranks vestibular schwannoma as most likely (medium–high). Conflict noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear and complete for a video visit; patient provided consistent symptom timeline and description.
  - Limitations: no physical exam possible via video and some medication details were uncertain (patient could not recall spray name).
